speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has posed a severe dilemma – summarised as lives versus livelihoods – for all regions in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When you close the borders and lock down society, you can save lives, but people will suffer tremendously from economic paralysis and children held back, perhaps permanently, in their learning.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When you open up society and the economy to resume normalcy quickly, many people will suffer from falling severely ill and die from infections.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Every region in the world knows it has to strike a very careful balance between lives and livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Three years into the pandemic, Singapore has been able to open up our society and economy, with life almost going back to normal and yet we maintain an excess mortality rate that is one of the lowest in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In September 2022, the Ministry of Health (MOH) released a public report on the excess deaths in the Singapore resident population over the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, our death rate during this pandemic, essentially, took us back to 2018 levels, wiping out improvements over a few years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The World Health Organization (WHO) uses a slightly different methodology to compute excess deaths, but the results are similar.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Based on WHO's estimates for the years 2020 and 2021, Singapore experienced 26 excess deaths per 100,000 persons per year, compared to our estimate, which was 24.9.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But it is still, again, much lower than many countries, especially those that have opened up like us.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Members have asked for a breakdown of the numbers by year.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, if we break up our estimated excess deaths, there were 1,140 from January 2020 to December 2021 and 1,350 from January to June 2022 respectively.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are two key ways to reduce excess deaths associated with the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: COVID-19 vaccination plays a big part because it significantly reduces the risk that infections translate into severe illness and deaths.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The fact that Singapore got 93% of its population vaccinated – and that base includes children who are not eligible – and 80% boosted, is a key reason why we have low excess deaths.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To answer Mr Yip Hon Weng's question, which has been scheduled for another Sitting, in the same vein, in Singapore and elsewhere in the world, unvaccinated persons disproportionately contributed to COVID-19 deaths.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOH does not comprehensively track the number of persons who are medically ineligible for COVID-19 vaccinations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, as at 30 June this year, the number of persons who applied to be exempted from vaccination-differentiated safe management measures (VDS), claimed they have adverse reactions to COVID-19 vaccines and we have looked at them and have granted 2,100 such exemptions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Again, this is the group which applied to be exempted from VDS.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In reality, the number of people who are medically ineligible for COVID-19 vaccines is small, given the choice of vaccines that they have access to.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is worth reiterating here that, to be properly protected against the Omicron virus of COVID-19, we need to get a booster, in other words, three doses of mRNA vaccines.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will reduce the risk of severe illnesses and deaths significantly.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Two shots do not do the job properly.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are currently bringing in the updated bivalent vaccines that can offer better protection against variants.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second factor is whether the healthcare system had been overwhelmed at any point during the pandemic – the second factor for excess deaths. "Overwhelme" is not the same as hospitals being very busy, which ours have been and are still very busy. "Overwhelme" means there were so many severely ill COVID-19 patients that the hospitals ran out of beds, oxygen and medical staff to take care of them.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Whenever a bed or an equipment becomes available, doctors have the unenviable task of choosing whom they should save amongst everyone that is waiting.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When that happens, many non-COVID-19 patients, such as those with heart attacks, injuries, strokes will be affected and, without proper care, many of them will also die.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In Singapore, we did not let that happen, mostly because when there was a risk of that happening, we went into the circuit breaker mode or the heightened alert mode to slow down the rate of infection to protect our healthcare system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, throughout the pandemic, despite our public hospitals being strained while coping with the pandemic, our hospital and ICU beds were able to support patients with urgent medical needs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Looking ahead, we can continue to prevent deaths by preserving healthcare capacity and ensuring that our healthcare workers are well-resourced in such situations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If and when there is a surge in infection and severe illness numbers, we cannot rule out the re-imposition of safe management measures.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But we will only do so when it is absolutely necessary to save lives and to protect the healthcare system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What we managed to achieve is due to the fact that the great majority of our people did their part and did the right thing.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The pandemic is not entirely over, but we hope we are at the end game and will continue to navigate through the crisis with resilience and unity.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Does the Government have plans to study more deeply the impact of socioeconomic status as well as housing type on the excess mortality risks from COVID-19?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have the Saw Swee Hock School of Public Health.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Notwithstanding, it is an interesting line of enquiry which our researchers will definitely look at.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, with more data, does MOH intend to periodically review the vaccination eligibility criteria to allow more people who were previously ineligible for vaccination to get vaccinated and protection from COVID-19?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, how does MOH intend to increase the vaccination rate, especially amongst those who are seniors and have comorbidities?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On vaccination eligibility, the question is actually the other way around.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We would very much want people to be vaccinated but, usually, it is the resident who comes forward to say "I am not eligible.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I have got eczema, I have this, I have that".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And then some are not so valid medically; others we have to take a closer look, especially if they have some adverse reaction after their first shot and they then may become ineligible.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And that is a medical indication which we will have to respect, notwithstanding the fact that we bring in different types of vaccines now with different technological platforms and, hopefully, they will be able to take one of them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, how do we further increase the rate of vaccinations?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have to keep on explaining why it is beneficial to vaccinate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When we see more of our friends and relatives vaccinated, we also, notwithstanding some hesitancy, will get vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we have to bring vaccinations to the community, which we are still doing through our mobile teams.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And also for those who are not mobile and are stuck at home, we will go to their homes to provide the vaccination.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But, as mentioned in the House earlier, we are trying to move to a new definition of "up to date" vaccination.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Whoever is holding out probably is very hesitant, unable to change their mind or, indeed, have medical contraindications and you cannot vaccinate them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Every year, when there is a season, take an influenza vaccination that will protect you throughout the year and we need to.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As we gather more data, as we have the shipments in and operations are ready, we will announce the details and move to a new mode of vaccinating the population.
